The question of whether organic food is better for the environment is genuinely contested, with research and expert opinion pointing in different directions depending on the metric considered. Sources such as the FAO [d3], the Better Health Channel [d7], and the Soil Association [d6] argue that organic farming reduces groundwater pollution, improves soil health through crop rotations and organic fertilizers, uses less energy, and could cut agricultural emissions by 40–50% in Europe by 2050. Similarly, [d4] states that organic farming practices "may reduce pollution, conserve water, reduce soil erosion, increase soil fertility, and use less energy." However, other credible sources directly challenge this view: Our World in Data [d5] concludes that "across several metrics, organic agriculture actually proves to be more harmful for the world's environment than conventional agriculture," and GreenBiz [d9] reports that organic farms require 25 to 110 percent more land to produce the same amount of food, creating a significant "carbon opportunity cost" by displacing natural ecosystems. A New York Times analysis [d10] adds that shifting all U.S. agriculture to organic would require converting an area larger than California from pristine land, and Scientific American [d11] notes that factory organic farms "use their own barrage of chemicals that are still ecologically damaging." In short, organic farming offers real environmental benefits in some areas (soil health, pesticide reduction, water quality) [d3][d4][d7], but these must be weighed against serious drawbacks in land use and overall emissions efficiency [d5][d9][d10][d11], making the answer highly dependent on which environmental metric is prioritized.
